keyEvents.title: Autonomy Vote
keyEvents.description: Comoros votes to remain part of the French Community with increased autonomy

independence.description: Comoros declared unilateral independence on July 6, 1975. However, Mayotte voted to remain French, creating a territorial dispute that persists to this day. The post-independence era was chaotic, defined by the influence of French mercenary Bob Denard, who organized multiple coups. The first president, Ahmed Abdallah, was overthrown within a month by the socialist revolutionary Ali Soilih. Soilih attempted radical modernization (burning archives, banning veils) before being killed in a counter-coup led by Denard in 1978, which reinstated Abdallah. The 'Mercenary Republic' lasted until 1989. The 1990s saw separatist movements in Anjouan and Mohéli, leading to the brink of disintegration.

keyEvents.title: Unilateral Independence
keyEvents.description: Ahmed Abdallah declares independence; Mayotte remains under French administration

keyEvents.title: Ali Soilih Regime
keyEvents.description: A radical socialist period attempting to modernize society, ended by a mercenary coup

keyEvents.title: Separatist Crisis

modern.description: To end the cycle of coups and separatism, a new constitution was ratified in 2001, creating the 'Union of the Comoros.' This system granted significant autonomy to each island and rotated the presidency between them every four years. While this brought relative stability and the first peaceful transfer of power in 2006, tensions remain. In 2008, the African Union invaded Anjouan to remove a renegade leader. Recent years have seen constitutional referendums strengthening the central power of President Azali Assoumani, sparking controversy and opposition, yet the nation continues to seek economic development through tourism and regional integration.

name: São Tomé and Príncipe
overview: São Tomé and Príncipe, Africa's second-smallest nation, has a history defined by its role as a plantation laboratory. Discovered uninhabited by the Portuguese in the 1470s, it became the world's leading sugar producer in the 16th century and later a hub for the transatlantic slave trade. The islands' fertile volcanic soil subsequently fueled coffee and cocoa cycles, earning them the nickname 'The Chocolate Islands,' but also a legacy of brutal contract labor. Since independence in 1975, the nation has transitioned from a socialist one-party state to a functioning multi-party democracy, balancing its colonial heritage with a distinct Creole 'Forro' identity.

source.label: Wikipedia - History of São Tomé and Príncipe

colonial.description: Portuguese navigators João de Santarém and Pêro Escobar discovered the uninhabited islands around 1470. Settlement began in 1493 with 'undesirables' and Jewish children expelled from Portugal, alongside enslaved Africans. By the mid-16th century, the islands were the world's largest sugar producer, a model later replicated in Brazil. However, slave revolts—most famously by Rei Amador in 1595—and competition from Brazil led to economic decline. The islands then served primarily as a slave trade entrepôt until the 19th century, when coffee and cocoa were introduced. The 'roça' (plantation) system revived the economy, making the islands the world's top cocoa producer by 1908. Despite the abolition of slavery, the 'serviçais' (contract labor) system remained notoriously brutal, famously exposed as 'modern slavery' by British journalists. The 1953 Batepá Massacre, where colonial authorities brutally suppressed a labor protest, ignited the nationalist movement.

independence.description: Following the 1974 Carnation Revolution in Portugal, the Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe (MLSTP) negotiated independence, which was achieved on July 12, 1975. Manuel Pinto da Costa became the first president. The new regime established a Marxist-Leninist one-party state, nationalizing the cocoa plantations. This period saw strong ties with Cuba and the Eastern Bloc but also economic stagnation as cocoa production plummeted due to mismanagement and the exodus of skilled Portuguese management. By the late 1980s, facing economic collapse and changing global winds, the government began a gradual transition toward democracy.

modern.description: In 1990, a new constitution was approved, instituting multi-party democracy. The 1991 elections saw the defeat of the MLSTP and the election of Miguel Trovoada, marking one of Africa's first peaceful democratic transitions. The modern era has been characterized by a functioning, albeit fragile, democracy with alternating power between parties. The economy remains dependent on international aid and cocoa exports, though hopes have been pinned on offshore oil exploration in the Gulf of Guinea. The country faces challenges of poverty and debt but remains peaceful compared to many regional neighbors.
